implementerProof.how: The production code of this round is right on both of review round 6's defects, and I verified each: applyRead is gone from the tree, the retry's whole call graph reaches no intake call, and the migration test's new case fails with the exact constraint violation when phase_ended is taken out again. Two of the round's items are not met, and both are failures of proof rather than of code. Item 1's required control does not hold: the shipped test passes unchanged with applyRead restored, because it never records the issue and an unrecorded issue has no tree to linger. Item 3's guarantee is not in the code at all: a new row kind added as a mark compiles and is read as the ordinary kind, which is review round 6's defect over again, and I measured that rather than argued it. I wrote and pushed the tests that pin item 1 and close the architect's extra check on A6; item 3's fix is the architect's decision and is in the review-rounds document.

failures.criterion: Item 1 - a refuse-once test for the re-assert row, for each of done, backlog and icebox: the tree does not linger, and the re-assert is written. It must fail with the fix reverted.
failures.evidence: TestTheDaemonsReassertIsWrittenAfterDispatchRefusesItsFirstWrite (packages/daemon/internal/daemon/outbox_integration_test.go) does not fail with the fix reverted. In a scratch clone at a21224a8 I restored the applyRead call in writeStatus - intake.ApplyFact with intake.ReadIssue(read) and r.handlers, exactly as round 6 found it - and ran the test: PASS on all three cases, identical to the head. Command: cd packages/daemon && go test ./internal/daemon/ -count=1 -run 'TestTheDaemonsReassertIsWrittenAfterDispatchRefusesItsFirstWrite' -v. The cause is that the test never records the issue: its only linger assertion is outboxRowsOf(t, pool, tc.key) == 0, and an issue the record knows nothing of has no tree to linger and no phase to move, so that count is 0 whether or not the read reaches the engine. The half of the test that does bite is the other half, the status written and the sequence it is written at; the half item 1 names, 'the tree does not linger', is vacuous as written. I have pinned it rather than only reported it: TestAReassertLeavesItsRecordedIssueInTheWorkflow, in packages/daemon/internal/daemon/reassert_no_linger_test.go, commit dc5fdfe0, records the issue in the workflow first - phase implementing, status in_progress, a tree of its own - and then asks the record itself. It passes all three cases at this head and fails all three with applyRead restored: 'reassert_no_linger_test.go:82: the recorded issue is out of the workflow at phase "done" status "done", want it still in: the retry's read reached the engine and the session's own done was taken for a person's', and the same for backlog and icebox. So the fix is right and something now proves it; what remains for the implementer is whether the shipped test should keep its vacuous assertion beside mine.

failures.criterion: Item 3 - each row kind's rule required by type, accepted as one switch whose default fails the row, provided a test proves an unknown kind fails loudly rather than borrowing another kind's rule.
failures.evidence: No such test exists, and through the public path none can, because the default that fails the row is unreachable. stillWanted's default does return an error, but stillWanted derives the kind itself from statusKindOf, whose own switch ends 'default: return ordinaryStatusRow'. That default is right for an ordinary row, which is the unmarked case, so the hole is in the other switch: a new kind is a new mark on record.StatusWrite, and a mark added without a case in statusKindOf compiles, is read as ordinaryStatusRow and is judged by statusStillWanted - which is review round 6's defect exactly, the re-assert judged by the ordinary rule. I measured it rather than reasoning about it. In a scratch clone at dc5fdfe0 I added a fourth kind the way a future one would arrive: a ProbeKind bool on record.StatusWrite and a probeRow const, with statusKindOf untouched. 'go build ./...' exits 0, so the compiler forces nothing. TestEveryStatusRowKindHasAStillWantedRule stays PASS, because its three cases are a hand-written table and a fourth kind is absent from it too - outbox.go's comment says that test 'holds to the list', and nothing holds the list to the kinds. And a probe over the real function prints 'statusKindOf of a marked payload with no case = 0 (ordinary=0, probe=3)', so the row takes the ordinary rule in silence. The decision's sentence 'A new row kind must name its rule, and the code does not compile without one' is therefore not true at this head. Commands: cd packages/daemon && go build ./... ; go test ./internal/daemon/ -count=1 -run 'TestProbeAFourthKindWithNoRuleBorrowsTheOrdinaryRule|TestEveryStatusRowKindHasAStillWantedRule' -v. The architect has since decided the fix - the row carries its Kind, set by one constructor per kind, statusKindOf and its fallback deleted, an empty or unknown kind failing the row, and a test walking the one list - and named this probe as its acceptance; I did not write the fix or a red test for it, since the shape it must take is now a design decision rather than a defect to pin.

proof.criterion: The architect's extra check 2 - the migration test's kind list is read from record.LaneKinds rather than kept by hand; confirm it would catch a kind missing from a future rewrite.
proof.surface: The source, read as a chain rather than at the one call.
proof.command: Compared the kind constants against the laneKinds map: extracted every 'OutboxKindX OutboxKind = "..."' constant and every kind named in the map, then comm -23 over the two sorted lists. Then read TestEveryOutboxKindIsInExactlyOneLane.
proof.observed: It would, and the reason is a chain rather than the LaneKinds call alone. 16 kinds are declared and all 16 are in the map - comm -23 prints nothing - and the test unions exactly the three lanes that exist (LaneLifecycle, LaneBoard, LaneRoleMessage), so its list is every kind today. What keeps it that way is TestEveryOutboxKindIsInExactlyOneLane: a kind must be on a lane to be queued and run at all, and that test ends with 'if len(lanes) != len(every)', so a kind added to a lane and not to its own hand-written list turns it red. A kind added to neither - a constant in no lane - is caught by nothing, but such a kind is never queued, so no rewrite can be violated by a row of it. The residual hand-kept thing is the lane list itself: a fourth lane would be missed by the migration test's union until someone added it there.
proof.negativeControl: The comm -23 is the control for the coverage claim: it prints the kinds in no lane, and prints nothing here, so the union really is every kind rather than a list that happens to be long enough.

Without that line the test would prove the state rather than the event.
